issues.item: Threat: Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
issues.explanation: 'Risky Behavior' is difficult to reconcile with the rest of the profile, which otherwise emphasizes hypervigilance, startle, danger in silence, fragmented/avoided trauma memory, and appraisals of betrayal and injustice after police violence. Those other items describe a fearful, threat-sensitive presentation; endorsing active risk-taking as a core threat item pulls in the opposite direction and is not supported elsewhere in the selected nodes.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself
issues.explanation: 'Can't Rely on Self' is a weaker fit than the other appraisals for this trauma/context. The profile is organized around external betrayal/injustice linked to police violence, but this item shifts to global self-distrust without corresponding self-blame, shame, incompetence, or strategy items elsewhere. In combination with the strong betrayal/injustice theme, it creates a less coherent appraisal profile.

vignette:
Javier has been a parole officer for thirty years, a career built on a belief in order, fairness, and the possibility of reform. At fifty-four, he carried himself with a quiet authority that most of his clients respected. But for the last eight months, that foundation has felt like sand. The story of how it all fell apart begins on a humid summer evening, not on the job, but on his own residential street. A dispute between two neighbors had escalated into shouting. Javier, off-duty and in a t-shirt and jeans, had gone out to mediate, his voice calm and steady as he’d done a thousand times before. He was making progress when the cruisers arrived, lights flashing but sirens off. The sudden, unnatural quiet that fell over the block was the last moment of peace he would know.

What happened next plays back in his mind not as a linear story, but as a series of brutal, disjointed snapshots. He remembers turning, hands slightly raised, to explain the situation to the responding officers. He remembers the blinding beam of a flashlight, a shove from behind, and the shocking, grinding pain of his face hitting the pavement. He can recall the weight of a knee in his back and the frantic, useless thumping of his own heart against his ribs, a sound so loud it seemed to drown out the confusing shouts. He remembers seeing the glint of another officer’s badge and the thought, sharp as glass, that these were his people, his colleagues in the same system of justice. The rest is a blur of fragments he can’t assemble. When he tries to force the memory into a coherent sequence, to see the faces or recall the exact words, a thick, protective wall rises in his mind, and he finds himself pushing it all away before the picture can become complete. The pieces he does hold feel so extreme, so utterly unbelievable, that he sometimes wonders if he imagined the sheer senselessness of it all.

This fractured memory now dictates the rhythm of his life. At the parole office, a place he once navigated with confidence, he is constantly on edge. He scans the faces in the waiting room, not for recognition, but for threats. He feels jumpy, startling violently when a clerk drops a heavy file on a desk. The most unnerving moments are the quiet ones. A lull in the usual office clamor, a moment of stillness before a parolee enters his office, fills him with a dreadful certainty that something dangerous is about to happen. This feeling is most potent when he is confronted with what he now sees everywhere: people misbehaving. A client showing up late with a defiant attitude, an argument breaking out in the hallway—these minor infractions trigger an immediate and overwhelming physical response. His heart begins to pound in his chest, that same frantic, trapped rhythm from the night on the pavement, and the room seems to shrink around him.

He has come to believe that the world is fundamentally unsafe and that the institutions designed to protect people are a lie. He dedicated his life to a system that, in his moment of need, had not only failed him but had actively harmed him. This sense of institutional failure is compounded by a deep, personal feeling of betrayal. These were men who wore a similar uniform, who should have been his brothers. The fact that the internal investigation went nowhere, that no one was held accountable, has become a constant, grinding source of bitterness. What happened to him was profoundly unfair, and the lack of any justice has left a permanent stain on his view of the world.

Over the months, he began to withdraw. He started passing off more volatile cases to junior officers, citing paperwork as an excuse. His wife, Elena, noticed he no longer sat with his back to the door in restaurants and that he would flinch at the sound of a passing siren. The final straw came last week. During a routine check-in with a low-risk parolee, the young man became agitated about a failed drug test. As his voice rose, Javier felt the familiar thunder in his chest, so intense this time that he was certain he was having a heart attack. He abruptly ended the meeting and spent the next hour in his car, waiting for his heart to slow down, drenched in sweat. It was Elena who made the appointment. Javier is here now because he is losing the career that defined him and because he feels like a stranger in his own life. He is terrified that speaking the story aloud will make the broken pieces whole and unbearable, but he is more terrified of what will happen if he doesn't.
